claim: Lin28a is expressed ubiquitously at E9.5 in mouse embryos.
source: At E9.5, Lin28a is expressed ubiquitously; and subsequently, its expression disappears from head to tail at around E10.5 and E11.5 (Yokoyama et al., 2008; Yokoyama et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Yokoyama et al., 2008; Yokoyama et al., 2009) and Figure 1A showing whole-mount in situ hybridization.

claim: Lin28a expression disappears from head to tail at around E10.5 and E11.5.
source: At E9.5, Lin28a is expressed ubiquitously; and subsequently, its expression disappears from head to tail at around E10.5 and E11.5 (Yokoyama et al., 2008; Yokoyama et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited references and Figure 1A showing spatiotemporal expression changes.

claim: Most Lin28a–/– mice died perinatally or within a few days after birth.
source: Most of the Lin28a–/– mice died perinatally or within a few days after birth (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1 showing survival frequencies.

claim: Lin28a–/– mice exhibited short stature compared with wild-type mice.
source: Lin28a–/– mice exhibited short stature compared with wild-type (Wt) mice and showed severe growth defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by visual comparison in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and body weight measurements.

claim: Lin28a is necessary for normal growth.
source: These findings are consistent with previous reports that Lin28a is necessary for normal growth (Shinoda et al., 2013); however, our Lin28a–/– mice showed severe phenotypes that might have been caused by differences in gene targeting construct and genetic background.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shinoda et al., 2013 and comparison with current study results.

claim: Lin28a–/– mice showed a slight anterior shift of the hindlimbs.
source: We then examined anteroposterior axis formation in Lin28a–/– mice since Lin28a–/– mice showed a slight anterior shift of the hindlimbs and shortened tails (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by visual observation in Figure 1B showing lateral views of embryos.

claim: Lin28a–/– mice showed shortened tails.
source: We then examined anteroposterior axis formation in Lin28a–/– mice since Lin28a–/– mice showed a slight anterior shift of the hindlimbs and shortened tails (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by visual observation in Figure 1B.

claim: The hindlimbs of Lin28a–/– mice shifted anteriorly by one somite (from the 23rd to the 28th expression domains of Myog).
source: The hindlimbs of Lin28a–/– mice shifted anteriorly by one somite (from the 23rd to the 28th expression domains of Myog), whereas the position of the forelimb buds of Lin28a–/– mice were not altered (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The position of the forelimb buds of Lin28a–/– mice were not altered.
source: The hindlimbs of Lin28a–/– mice shifted anteriorly by one somite (from the 23rd to the 28th expression domains of Myog), whereas the position of the forelimb buds of Lin28a–/– mice were not altered (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Tail bud-specific overexpression or knockout of Lin28a affects the number of caudal vertebrae.
source: These results are supported by previous reports that tail bud-specific overexpression or knockout of Lin28a affects the number of caudal vertebrae (Aires et al., 2019; Robinton et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aires et al., 2019 and Robinton et al., 2019.

claim: In Lin28a–/– mice, the anterior arch of the atlas was formed from the second cervical vertebra (C2).
source: In Lin28a–/– mice, the anterior arch of the atlas was formed from the second cervical vertebra (C2) (Figure 1D), and not from C1, as normally observed, or from the fusion of C1 and C2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Atlas transformations were observed in 64.3% of Lin28a–/– mice.
source: These transformations were observed in 64.3% of Lin28a–/– mice and in 21.1% of Lin28a+/– mice; in contrast, they were never found in Wt mice (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Table 1.

claim: Atlas transformations were observed in 21.1% of Lin28a+/– mice.
source: These transformations were observed in 64.3% of Lin28a–/– mice and in 21.1% of Lin28a+/– mice; in contrast, they were never found in Wt mice (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Table 1.

claim: Atlas transformations were never found in Wt mice.
source: These transformations were observed in 64.3% of Lin28a–/– mice and in 21.1% of Lin28a+/– mice; in contrast, they were never found in Wt mice (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Table 1.

claim: There were only six pairs of true ribs attached to the sternum in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: There were only six pairs of true ribs attached to the sternum in Lin28a–/– mice, whereas Wt and Lin28a+/– mice had seven pairs (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 1F.

claim: Wt and Lin28a+/– mice had seven pairs of true ribs attached to the sternum.
source: There were only six pairs of true ribs attached to the sternum in Lin28a–/– mice, whereas Wt and Lin28a+/– mice had seven pairs (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 1F.

claim: An abnormal number of ribs was observed in Lin28a–/– mice at 100% penetrance.
source: Furthermore, an abnormal number of ribs was observed in Lin28a–/– mice at 100% penetrance, whereas Wt and Lin28a+/– mice exhibited the normal 13 pairs of ribs (Figure 1G and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 1G and quantitative data in Table 1.

claim: Wt and Lin28a+/– mice exhibited the normal 13 pairs of ribs.
source: Furthermore, an abnormal number of ribs was observed in Lin28a–/– mice at 100% penetrance, whereas Wt and Lin28a+/– mice exhibited the normal 13 pairs of ribs (Figure 1G and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 1G and quantitative data in Table 1.

claim: Posterior transformations of vertebral identity occur in the 7th and 13th thoracic vertebrae during skeletal patterning in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: These results suggest that posterior transformations of vertebral identity occur in the 7th and 13th thoracic vertebrae during skeletal patterning.
evidence: Inferred from the observed rib abnormalities in Lin28a–/– mice.

claim: Partial transformations were observed in the first sacral vertebra (S1) in Lin28a–/– mice, producing a morphological feature of lumbar vertebrae on only one side.
source: Moreover, partial transformations were observed in the first sacral vertebra (S1), producing a morphological feature of lumbar vertebrae on only one side (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 1H.

claim: Lin28a plays a critical role in the specification of vertebrae along the anteroposterior axis.
source: Finally, Lin28a–/– mice showed various skeletal transformations (Figure 1I), suggesting that Lin28a plays a critical role in the specification of vertebrae along the anteroposterior axis.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple skeletal transformations observed in Lin28a–/– mice.

claim: Lin28a–/– mice exhibited global dysregulation of Hox genes at E9.5.
source: Lin28a–/– mice exhibited global dysregulation of Hox genes, which was most remarkable for the 5' (posterior) Hox genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The dysregulation of Hox genes in Lin28a–/– mice was most remarkable for the 5' (posterior) Hox genes.
source: Lin28a–/– mice exhibited global dysregulation of Hox genes, which was most remarkable for the 5' (posterior) Hox genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The expression domain of Hoxc13 was enlarged anteriorly in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: Whole-mount in situ hybridization analyses revealed that the expression domain of Hoxc13 and Hoxd12 was enlarged anteriorly (Figure 2B and C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression domain of Hoxd12 was enlarged anteriorly in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: Whole-mount in situ hybridization analyses revealed that the expression domain of Hoxc13 and Hoxd12 was enlarged anteriorly (Figure 2B and C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The short-tailed phenotype in Lin28a–/– mice might be caused by the anteriorization of Hox paralogous group 12 and 13 expression.
source: These results suggest that the short-tailed phenotype in Lin28a–/– mice might be caused by the anteriorization of Hox paralogous group 12 and 13 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observed anterior expansion of Hoxc13 and Hoxd12 expression domains.

claim: Hox genes are modulated by retinoic acid (RA) signaling.
source: It is known that Hox genes are modulated by retinoic acid (RA) signaling, and that RA exposure causes posterior transformations of vertebrae via global anteriorization of Hox gene expression (Kessel and Gruss, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kessel and Gruss, 1991.

claim: RA exposure causes posterior transformations of vertebrae via global anteriorization of Hox gene expression.
source: It is known that Hox genes are modulated by retinoic acid (RA) signaling, and that RA exposure causes posterior transformations of vertebrae via global anteriorization of Hox gene expression (Kessel and Gruss, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kessel and Gruss, 1991.

claim: Lin28a+/– mice that received RA treatment showed loss of the 13th pair of ribs.
source: Lin28a+/– mice that received RA treatment showed loss of the 13th pair of ribs, which coincided with the findings observed in Lin28a–/– mice, whereas no obvious defects were observed in Wt littermates (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 2D.

claim: No obvious defects were observed in Wt littermates that received RA treatment.
source: Lin28a+/– mice that received RA treatment showed loss of the 13th pair of ribs, which coincided with the findings observed in Lin28a–/– mice, whereas no obvious defects were observed in Wt littermates (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 2D.

claim: The severity of skeletal patterning defects in the cervical region correlated with the genotype of Lin28a after RA treatment.
source: In the cervical region, the severity of skeletal patterning defects correlated with the genotype of Lin28a (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–2F).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–2F.

claim: Perturbation of Hox genes by RA administration enhances the Lin28a+/- and -/- phenotypes.
source: These results show that perturbation of Hox genes by RA administration enhances the Lin28a+/- and -/- phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by the observed increased severity of skeletal defects after RA treatment in Lin28a mutants.

claim: Dysregulation of Hox genes is responsible for the skeletal patterning defects in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: In particular, since RA administration in Lin28a+/- mice results in the same phenotype as untreated Lin28a-/-, it is possible that dysregulation of Hox genes is responsible for the skeletal patterning defects in Lin28a–/– mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from the RA treatment experiments showing phenocopy of Lin28a–/– phenotypes.

claim: Lin28a is a negative regulator of let-7 biogenesis by interfering with Drosha processing of pri-let-7.
source: Since Lin28a is known as a negative regulator of let-7 biogenesis by interfering with Drosha processing of pri-let-7 (Newman et al., 2008; Viswanathan et al., 2008), and by TUT4-mediated terminal uridylation and inhibition of Dicer processing (Heo et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2013), we examined the microRNA expression profile of Lin28a–/– mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to Newman et al., 2008 and Viswanathan et al., 2008.

claim: Lin28a is a negative regulator of let-7 biogenesis by TUT4-mediated terminal uridylation and inhibition of Dicer processing.
source: Since Lin28a is known as a negative regulator of let-7 biogenesis by interfering with Drosha processing of pri-let-7 (Newman et al., 2008; Viswanathan et al., 2008), and by TUT4-mediated terminal uridylation and inhibition of Dicer processing (Heo et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2013), we examined the microRNA expression profile of Lin28a–/– mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to Heo et al., 2009 and Chang et al., 2013.

claim: Mature microRNAs of let-7-family members were significantly accumulated in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Viswanathan et al., 2008; Rybak et al., 2008), we found that mature microRNAs of let-7-family members were significantly accumulated in Lin28a–/– mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by TaqMan microRNA array analyses shown in Figure 3A and citations to Viswanathan et al., 2008 and Rybak et al., 2008.

claim: There was no difference between Wt and Lin28a–/– mice with regards to the expression of mir-10 and mir-196 family microRNAs.
source: There was no difference between Wt and Lin28a–/– mice with regards to the expression of either mir-10 and mir-196 family microRNAs, which are regulators of the spatial expression of Hox genes and of vertebral specification (Woltering and Durston, 2008; Yekta et al., 2004; Hornstein et al., 2005; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 3C.

claim: mir-10 and mir-196 family microRNAs are regulators of the spatial expression of Hox genes and of vertebral specification.
source: There was no difference between Wt and Lin28a–/– mice with regards to the expression of either mir-10 and mir-196 family microRNAs, which are regulators of the spatial expression of Hox genes and of vertebral specification (Woltering and Durston, 2008; Yekta et al., 2004; Hornstein et al., 2005; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Woltering and Durston, 2008; Yekta et al., 2004; and Hornstein et al., 2005.

claim: The ablation of Lin28a promotes the specific accumulation of let-7 family microRNAs during embryogenesis.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Heo et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2013), these results imply that the ablation of Lin28a promotes the specific accumulation of let-7 family microRNAs during embryogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observed accumulation of let-7 in Lin28a–/– mice and supported by citations.

claim: Cbx2, Cbx5, and E2f6 are direct targets of let-7.
source: While these results in HEK293T cells with partial 3'UTR sequences do not completely exclude the possibility that Dusp4 and Arl4d are not target genes of let-7, they do suggest that Cbx2, Cbx5 and E2f6 are direct targets of let-7 (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Cbx2 was the only gene that was significantly downregulated in Lin28a-/- embryos and its expression was affected in a let-7-dependent manner.
source: Protein expression analyses revealed that Cbx2 was the only gene that was significantly downregulated in Lin28a-/- embryos, and also its expression was affected in a let-7-dependent manner (Figure 3F and H).
evidence: Supported by western blot analyses shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Cbx2 is a molecular target of the Lin28a/let-7 pathway in skeletal patterning.
source: These findings suggest that Cbx2 is, at least in part, a molecular target of the Lin28a/let-7 pathway in skeletal patterning.
evidence: Inferred from the luciferase assay and protein expression analyses showing let-7-dependent regulation of Cbx2.

claim: Cbx2 is one of the PcG genes that regulates Hox genes via histone modification.
source: Cbx2 is one of the PcG genes that regulates Hox genes via histone modification, and ablation of Cbx2 shows skeletal patterning defects in mice (Core et al., 1997; Nielsen et al., 2001; Courel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Core et al., 1997; Nielsen et al., 2001; and Courel et al., 2008.

claim: Ablation of Cbx2 shows skeletal patterning defects in mice.
source: Cbx2 is one of the PcG genes that regulates Hox genes via histone modification, and ablation of Cbx2 shows skeletal patterning defects in mice (Core et al., 1997; Nielsen et al., 2001; Courel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Core et al., 1997; Nielsen et al., 2001; and Courel et al., 2008.

claim: Cbx2 homozygous mutants exhibited skeletal patterning defects including fusion of C1 and C2 vertebrae.
source: The Cbx2 homozygous mutants exhibited skeletal patterning defects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–1E): fusion of C1 and C2 vertebrae, additional rib formation from the 7th cervical vertebra, T1 to T2 transformation of the spinous process, and 13th rib truncation.
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–1E.

claim: Double heterozygous mutants of Lin28a and Cbx2 showed ablation or truncation of the 13th pair of ribs.
source: The double heterozygous mice showed ablation or truncation of the 13th pair of ribs, although the Lin28+/– and Cbx2+/– single mutants did not show any obvious phenotypic irregularities (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 3I and quantitative data in Figure 3J.

claim: Lin28+/– and Cbx2+/– single mutants did not show any obvious phenotypic irregularities.
source: The double heterozygous mice showed ablation or truncation of the 13th pair of ribs, although the Lin28+/– and Cbx2+/– single mutants did not show any obvious phenotypic irregularities (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by skeletal preparation images in Figure 3I and quantitative data in Figure 3J.

claim: Decreased expression of Cbx2 enhances the Lin28a+/- phenotypes.
source: These results show that decreased expression of Cbx2 enhances the Lin28a+/- phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by the genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced phenotypes in double heterozygous mutants.

claim: Genetic interactions exist between Lin28a and Cbx2.
source: Together, these results indicate that let-7 directly regulates Cbx2, and that genetic interactions exist between Lin28a and Cbx2.
evidence: Supported by the double heterozygous mutant phenotypes.

claim: Lin28a/let-7 reciprocal feedback regulates Cbx2 expression.
source: Furthermore, they suggest that Lin28a/let-7 reciprocal feedback regulates Cbx2 expression, and that this pathway contributes to the regulation of proper skeletal patterning during embryogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of let-7 accumulation, Cbx2 downregulation, and genetic interactions.

claim: The Lin28a/let-7/Cbx2 pathway contributes to the regulation of proper skeletal patterning during embryogenesis.
source: Furthermore, they suggest that Lin28a/let-7 reciprocal feedback regulates Cbx2 expression, and that this pathway contributes to the regulation of proper skeletal patterning during embryogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results showing the pathway's effects on skeletal development.

claim: Hox gene expression is epigenetically restricted to unique spatiotemporal patterns during embryogenesis by PcG genes.
source: Hox gene expression is epigenetically restricted to unique spatiotemporal patterns during embryogenesis by PcG genes (Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009.

claim: The promoter regions of Hoxa3, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, Hoxa11, and Hoxa13 exhibited a high concentration of histone H3K27me3 in Wt embryos.
source: We found the promoter regions of Hoxa3, Hoxa9, Hoxa10, Hoxa11, and Hoxa13 exhibited a high concentration of histone H3K27me3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP and q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For histone H3 modifications, both K27me3 and K4me3 were not altered in Lin28a–/– embryos compared with Wt.
source: We found that for histone H3 modifications, both K27me4 and K4me3 were not altered in Lin28a–/– embryos compared with Wt (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP and q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: There was at least a two-fold reduction of Cbx2 binding at posterior Hox regions in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: Consistent with the expression level of Cbx2 (Figure 3G), we found at least a two-fold reduction of its binding at posterior Hox regions in Lin28a–/– mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP and q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The occupancy of Ring1b was reduced in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: Intriguingly, the occupancy of Ring1b, another component of PRC1 (Suzuki et al., 2002), and H2AK119 ubiquitination (H2AK119ub) which is catalyzed by Ring1b (Suzuki et al., 2002), were also reduced in Lin28a–/– mice (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP and q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 4F.

claim: H2AK119 ubiquitination was reduced in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: Intriguingly, the occupancy of Ring1b, another component of PRC1 (Suzuki et al., 2002), and H2AK119 ubiquitination (H2AK119ub) which is catalyzed by Ring1b (Suzuki et al., 2002), were also reduced in Lin28a–/– mice (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP and q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Ring1b is a component of PRC1.
source: Intriguingly, the occupancy of Ring1b, another component of PRC1 (Suzuki et al., 2002), and H2AK119 ubiquitination (H2AK119ub) which is catalyzed by Ring1b (Suzuki et al., 2002), were also reduced in Lin28a–/– mice (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suzuki et al., 2002.

claim: H2AK119 ubiquitination is catalyzed by Ring1b.
source: Intriguingly, the occupancy of Ring1b, another component of PRC1 (Suzuki et al., 2002), and H2AK119 ubiquitination (H2AK119ub) which is catalyzed by Ring1b (Suzuki et al., 2002), were also reduced in Lin28a–/– mice (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suzuki et al., 2002.

claim: The Lin28a/let-7 axis plays a critical role in PcG-mediated Hox gene repression.
source: Because each posterior Hox gene (Hoxa11, Hoxc13, and Hoxd12) is located on distinct chromosomes, these results indicate a critical role for the Lin28a/let-7 axis in PcG-mediated Hox gene repression.
evidence: Inferred from the observed reduction in PRC1 occupancy at multiple Hox loci on different chromosomes.

claim: Cbx2 repression by let-7 leads to the reduction of PRC1 occupancy at the Hox loci and the transcriptional initiation of posterior Hox genes.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that Cbx2 repression by let-7 leads to the reduction of PRC1 occupancy at the Hox loci and the transcriptional initiation of posterior Hox genes (Figure 4H).
evidence: Inferred from the combined ChIP and expression data.

claim: Lin28a–/– ES-like cells showed high alkaline phosphatase activity.
source: These colonies showed high alkaline phosphatase activity (Figure 5A) and also expressed pluripotent factors (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lin28a–/– ES-like cells expressed pluripotent factors.
source: These colonies showed high alkaline phosphatase activity (Figure 5A) and also expressed pluripotent factors (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Global accumulation of let-7-family microRNAs was observed in Lin28a–/– ES-like cells.
source: As observed in Lin28a–/– embryos (Figure 3B), global accumulation of let-7-family microRNAs was observed in the mutant cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Hox genes were upregulated upon differentiation in embryoid bodies derived from Lin28a–/– ES-like cells.
source: Hox genes were upregulated upon differentiation in these embryoid bodies, suggesting that a recapitulation of the Hox gene upregulation observed in Lin28a–/– mice occurred in Lin28a–/– ES-like cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Dysregulation of Hoxa11 and Hoxd12 was rescued in Lin28a–/–; let-7KD clones.
source: qPCR analysis revealed that dysregulation of Hoxa11 and Hoxd12 was rescued in Lin28a–/–; let-7KD clones (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Decreasing Cbx2 protein expression level in embryoid bodies-derived Lin28a–/– ES-like cells was rescued by knock down of let-7.
source: Moreover, we also confirmed that a decreasing Cbx2 protein expression level in embryoid bodies-derived Lin28a–/– ES-like cells was rescued by knock down of let-7 (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by western blot analyses shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Hoxa11 and Hoxd12 were up-regulated in Lin28a–/– cells, and this abnormal expression was absent in Lin28a–/–; Cbx2 3'UTR mutant cells.
source: Consistent with the result of let-7 knock down (Figure 5G–I), we found that Hoxa11 and Hoxd12 were up-regulated in Lin28a–/– cells, and that this abnormal expression was absent in Lin28a–/–; Cbx2 3'UTR mutant cells (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses shown in Figure 5K.

claim: let-7-mediated Cbx2 repression is responsible for Hox gene dysregulation in Lin28a–/– mice.
source: These results suggest that let-7-mediated Cbx2 repression is, at least in part, responsible for Hox gene dysregulation in Lin28a–/– mice.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing restoration of normal Hox gene expression when let-7 is knocked down or Cbx2 3'UTR is mutated.

claim: The Lin28a/let-7 pathway is involved in skeletal patterning via Polycomb-mediated Hox gene regulation.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the upregulation of let-7 leads to decreased PRC1 occupancy, which causes the disruption of the 'Hox code,' thus indicating the potential role of the Lin28a/let-7 pathway in skeletal patterning via Polycomb-mediated Hox gene regulation (Figure 5L).
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of all experiments showing the pathway from Lin28a through let-7 and Cbx2 to Hox gene regulation.

claim: The body plan along the anteroposterior axis is modulated by the spatiotemporal expression of Hox genes, which is known as the 'Hox code'.
source: The body plan along the anteroposterior axis is modulated by the spatiotemporal expression of Hox genes, which is known as the 'Hox code' (Wellik, 2007; Mallo and Alonso, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wellik, 2007 and Mallo and Alonso, 2013.

claim: Hox genes encode a family of transcription factors that contain a helix-turn-helix type homeodomain.
source: Hox genes encode a family of transcription factors that contain a helix-turn-helix type homeodomain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hox genes.

claim: In vertebrates, Hox genes are organized into four paralogous clusters (A to D).
source: In vertebrates, Hox genes are organized into four paralogous clusters (A to D) that can be divided into thirteen groups.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hox gene organization.

claim: The members of each paralogous group have partially redundant functions, but also acquire independent functions.
source: The members of each paralogous group have partially redundant functions, but also acquire independent functions (Wellik, 2007; Mallo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wellik, 2007 and Mallo et al., 2010.

claim: During development, the paralogous group at the 3' end of the clusters is expressed in the anterior part of the body.
source: During development, the paralogous group at the 3' end of the clusters is expressed in the anterior part of the body, while the more 5' genes are expressed in the more posterior part, towards the tail (Deschamps and van Nes, 2005; Dressler and Gruss, 1989; Duboule and Dollé, 1989; Gaunt and Strachan, 1996; Graham et al., 1989; Izpisúa-Belmonte et al., 1991b; Izpisúa-Belmonte et al., 1991a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing Hox gene expression patterns.

claim: The more 5' Hox genes are expressed in the more posterior part, towards the tail.
source: During development, the paralogous group at the 3' end of the clusters is expressed in the anterior part of the body, while the more 5' genes are expressed in the more posterior part, towards the tail (Deschamps and van Nes, 2005; Dressler and Gruss, 1989; Duboule and Dollé, 1989; Gaunt and Strachan, 1996; Graham et al., 1989; Izpisúa-Belmonte et al., 1991b; Izpisúa-Belmonte et al., 1991a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing Hox gene expression patterns.

claim: Hox gene-knockout mice show anterior transformations where specific vertebrae mimic the morphology of a more anterior one.
source: Hox gene-knockout mice show anterior transformations where specific vertebrae mimic the morphology of a more anterior one (Chisaka and Capecchi, 1991; Chisaka et al., 1992; Le Mouellic et al., 1992; Condie and Capecchi, 1993; Jeannotte et al., 1993; Small and Potter, 1993; Davis and Capecchi, 1994; Horan et al., 1994; Horan et al., 1995b; Horan et al., 1995a; Kostic and Capecchi, 1994; Davis et al., 1995; Rancourt et al., 1995; Suemori et al., 1995; Boulet and Capecchi, 1996; Fromental-Ramain et al., 1996b; Fromental-Ramain et al., 1996a; Carpenter et al., 1997; Chen and Capecchi, 1997; Chen et al., 1998; Manley and Capecchi, 1997; van den Akker et al., 2001; Garcia-Gasca and Spyropoulos, 2000; Wahba et al., 2001; Wellik and Capecchi, 2003; McIntyre et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to Hox knockout studies.

claim: Multistage controls, such as transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and epigenetic regulation, are required for the nested expression patterns of Hox genes.
source: Multistage controls, such as transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and epigenetic regulation, are required for the nested expression patterns of Hox genes (Mallo and Alonso, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mallo and Alonso, 2013.

claim: Polycomb group (PcG) genes are involved in Hox gene regulation via the chromatin architecture at Hox cluster loci in a developmental time-dependent manner.
source: As for epigenetic control, Polycomb group (PcG) genes are involved in Hox gene regulation via the chromatin architecture at Hox cluster loci in a developmental time-dependent manner (Soshnikova, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Soshnikova, 2014.

claim: PcG genes form two complexes, the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC) one and PRC2.
source: PcG genes form two complexes, the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC) one and PRC2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PcG complexes.

claim: PRC2 includes Ezh2, which can catalyze H3K27me3 at target loci.
source: PRC2 includes Ezh2, which can catalyze H3K27me3 at target loci, and consequently, this specific histone modification causes the recruitment of PRC1 via Cbx2 in the complex to silence gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRC2 function.

claim: H3K27me3 histone modification causes the recruitment of PRC1 via Cbx2 in the complex to silence gene expression.
source: PRC2 includes Ezh2, which can catalyze H3K27me3 at target loci, and consequently, this specific histone modification causes the recruitment of PRC1 via Cbx2 in the complex to silence gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRC1 recruitment.

claim: The accumulation of PcG complexes at Hox clusters during embryogenesis leads to the transcriptional silencing of Hox genes.
source: Thus, the accumulation of PcG complexes at Hox clusters during embryogenesis leads to the transcriptional silencing of Hox genes, which is supported by evidence that the ablation of PcG genes dysregulates Hox gene expression, resulting in subsequent skeletal transformation in anteroposterior patterning (Mallo and Alonso, 2013; Soshnikova, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mallo and Alonso, 2013 and Soshnikova, 2014.

claim: The ablation of PcG genes dysregulates Hox gene expression, resulting in subsequent skeletal transformation in anteroposterior patterning.
source: Thus, the accumulation of PcG complexes at Hox clusters during embryogenesis leads to the transcriptional silencing of Hox genes, which is supported by evidence that the ablation of PcG genes dysregulates Hox gene expression, resulting in subsequent skeletal transformation in anteroposterior patterning (Mallo and Alonso, 2013; Soshnikova, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mallo and Alonso, 2013 and Soshnikova, 2014.

claim: During embryogenesis, PcG gene expression gradually diminishes.
source: During embryogenesis, PcG gene expression gradually diminishes (Hashimoto et al., 1998), which leads to the initiation of spatiotemporal Hox gene expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hashimoto et al., 1998.

claim: The gradual diminishment of PcG gene expression leads to the initiation of spatiotemporal Hox gene expression.
source: During embryogenesis, PcG gene expression gradually diminishes (Hashimoto et al., 1998), which leads to the initiation of spatiotemporal Hox gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between PcG expression and Hox gene activation.

claim: Lin-28 was identified as a heterochronic gene that regulates the developmental timing of multiple organs in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Lin-28 was identified as a heterochronic gene that regulates the developmental timing of multiple organs in Caenorhabditis elegans (C.elegans) (Moss et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss et al., 1997.

claim: Lin-28 encodes an RNA-binding protein.
source: Lin-28 encodes an RNA-binding protein, and the loss of function of Lin-28 causes precocious development, with skipping of events that are specific to the second larval stage (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984; Moss et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ambros and Horvitz, 1984 and Moss et al., 1997.

claim: The loss of function of Lin-28 causes precocious development in C. elegans, with skipping of events that are specific to the second larval stage.
source: Lin-28 encodes an RNA-binding protein, and the loss of function of Lin-28 causes precocious development, with skipping of events that are specific to the second larval stage (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984; Moss et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ambros and Horvitz, 1984 and Moss et al., 1997.

claim: Mutants of let-7 exhibit reiteration of the fourth larval developmental stage because of failures in terminal differentiation and cell-cycle exit.
source: In contrast, mutants of let-7, a microRNA-encoding heterochronic gene, exhibit reiteration of the fourth larval developmental stage because of failures in terminal differentiation and cell-cycle exit (Pasquinelli et al., 2000; Reinhart et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pasquinelli et al., 2000 and Reinhart et al., 2000.

claim: Lin-28 and let-7 form a negative feedback loop that is essential for developmental timing in C. elegans.
source: Importantly, Lin-28 and let-7 form a negative feedback loop that is essential for developmental timing in C. elegans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Lin-28/let-7 relationship in C. elegans.

claim: The reciprocal regulation between Lin28a and let-7 is well conserved in mammals.
source: This reciprocal regulation between Lin28a and let-7 is well conserved in mammals (Moss and Tang, 2003; Viswanathan et al., 2008); Lin28a promotes the degradation of let-7 precursors (Heo et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2013), whereas let-7 inhibits Lin28a expression via posttranscriptional regulation (Moss and Tang, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moss and Tang, 2003 and Viswanathan et al., 2008.

claim: Lin28a promotes the degradation of let-7 precursors.
source: This reciprocal regulation between Lin28a and let-7 is well conserved in mammals (Moss and Tang, 2003; Viswanathan et al., 2008); Lin28a promotes the degradation of let-7 precursors (Heo et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2013), whereas let-7 inhibits Lin28a expression via posttranscriptional regulation (Moss and Tang, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heo et al., 2009 and Chang et al., 2013.

claim: let-7 inhibits Lin28a expression via posttranscriptional regulation.
source: This reciprocal regulation between Lin28a and let-7 is well conserved in mammals (Moss and Tang, 2003; Viswanathan et al., 2008); Lin28a promotes the degradation of let-7 precursors (Heo et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2013), whereas let-7 inhibits Lin28a expression via posttranscriptional regulation (Moss and Tang, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss and Tang, 2003.

claim: Vertebrates possess two homologs of Lin28 genes, Lin28a and Lin28b.
source: Vertebrates possess two homologs of Lin28 genes, Lin28a and Lin28b.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Lin28 genes in vertebrates.

claim: Lin28a is highly expressed in pluripotent stem cells.
source: Lin28a is highly expressed in pluripotent stem cells and is ubiquitously expressed in the early embryonic stage, and its expression is diminished during development (Yang and Moss, 2003; Shyh-Chang and Daley, 2013; Yokoyama et al., 2008; Yokoyama et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang and Moss, 2003; Shyh-Chang and Daley, 2013; Yokoyama et al., 2008; and Yokoyama et al., 2009.

claim: Lin28a is ubiquitously expressed in the early embryonic stage, and its expression is diminished during development.
source: Lin28a is highly expressed in pluripotent stem cells and is ubiquitously expressed in the early embryonic stage, and its expression is diminished during development (Yang and Moss, 2003; Shyh-Chang and Daley, 2013; Yokoyama et al., 2008; Yokoyama et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang and Moss, 2003; Shyh-Chang and Daley, 2013; Yokoyama et al., 2008; and Yokoyama et al., 2009.

claim: Lin28b is dominantly expressed in testes, placenta, and fetal liver, as well as in undifferentiated hepatocarcinoma.
source: In contrast, Lin28b is dominantly expressed in testes, placenta, and fetal liver, as well as in undifferentiated hepatocarcinoma (Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2006.

claim: Lin28a has versatile functions in diverse events, such as germ layer formation, germ cell development, neural development, glucose metabolism, and skeletal development.
source: The versatile functions of Lin28a are observed in diverse events, such as germ layer formation (Faas et al., 2013), germ cell development (West et al., 2009), neural development (Yang et al., 2015), glucose metabolism (Zhu et al., 2011), and skeletal development (Aires et al., 2019; Robinton et al., 2019; Papaioannou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on Lin28a functions.

claim: let-7-family genes are highly expressed in differentiated tissues.
source: Conversely, let-7-family genes are highly expressed in differentiated tissues, and their products function as tumor suppressors via the inhibition of oncogenes such as c-Myc, K-ras, and Hmga2 (Mayr et al., 2007; Lee and Dutta, 2007; Johnson et al., 2005; Sampson et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayr et al., 2007; Lee and Dutta, 2007; Johnson et al., 2005; and Sampson et al., 2007.

claim: let-7 products function as tumor suppressors via the inhibition of oncogenes such as c-Myc, K-ras, and Hmga2.
source: Conversely, let-7-family genes are highly expressed in differentiated tissues, and their products function as tumor suppressors via the inhibition of oncogenes such as c-Myc, K-ras, and Hmga2 (Mayr et al., 2007; Lee and Dutta, 2007; Johnson et al., 2005; Sampson et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayr et al., 2007; Lee and Dutta, 2007; Johnson et al., 2005; and Sampson et al., 2007.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of the human LIN28B locus correlated with height and the timing of menarche.
source: In addition to Lin28a, Lin28b regulates let-7 biogenesis, and it is known that single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) of the human LIN28B locus correlated with height and the timing of menarche (Lettre et al., 2008; Perry et al., 2009; He et al., 2009; Ong et al., 2009; Widén et al., 2010; Sulem et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lettre et al., 2008; Perry et al., 2009; He et al., 2009; Ong et al., 2009; Widén et al., 2010; and Sulem et al., 2009.

claim: The Lin28a/let-7 pathway is critical for axial elongation.
source: In this study, we demonstrated that the Lin28a/let-7 pathway is critical for axial elongation.
evidence: Supported by the observed shortened tails and skeletal transformations in Lin28a–/– mice.

claim: The accumulation of let-7 in Lin28a–/– mice resulted in the reduction of PRC1 occupancy at the Hox cluster loci by targeting Cbx2.
source: The accumulation of let-7 in Lin28a–/– mice resulted in the reduction of PRC1 occupancy at the Hox cluster loci by targeting Cbx2.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analyses showing reduced PRC1 occupancy and luciferase assays showing let-7 targeting of Cbx2.

claim: Lin28a loss in embryonic stem-like cells led to aberrant induction of posterior Hox genes, which was rescued by the knockdown of let-7.
source: Consistently, Lin28a loss in embryonic stem-like cells led to aberrant induction of posterior Hox genes, which was rescued by the knockdown of let-7.
evidence: Supported by q-PCR analyses showing Hox gene upregulation in Lin28a–/– ES cells and rescue upon let-7 knockdown.

claim: The Lin28/let-7 pathway is involved in the modulation of the 'Hox code' via Polycomb regulation during axial patterning.
source: These results suggest that the Lin28/let-7 pathway is involved in the modulation of the 'Hox code' via Polycomb regulation during axial patterning.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental results presented in the study.
